source: Written by Claude (claude-opus-5-5) from the county counts (AP via The New York Times), the 2024 baseline and Census ACS 2023 context.

20067.t:
Grant County stayed solidly Republican in the U.S. Senate race but shifted sharply. Marshall beat Hamilton 1,066 to 498, a 35-point margin, down from Trump's 63-point win over Harris in 2024. That 28-point move toward the Democrats ranks fourth among Kansas's 105 counties, all of which moved left. It is well above the typical move of 18 points in the state and 14 nationally. Counties with similar 2024 margins moved less: Stafford by 20 points, Harper by 16 and Doniphan by 16.

Only 1,617 votes were cast, 73% of the 2024 total. The count cannot tell how much of the shift came from voters changing their minds and how much from voters staying home.

20033.t:
In the U.S. Senate race, Comanche County stayed firmly Republican for Marshall but moved 21 points toward Hamilton, the Democrat, compared with the 2024 presidential vote. Trump carried it by 68 points; Marshall won it by 47, with 446 votes to 149. That move nearly matched the state's own 21-point shift, which carried Hamilton to a 5-point statewide win, and it beat the typical Kansas county's 18 points and the national typical 14. Similar small, deeply Republican counties moved somewhat less: Kearny 16 points, Hamilton County 18, Cheyenne 15.

Only 628 votes were cast, 72% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20163.t:
Rooks County stayed firmly Republican in the U.S. Senate race, though by less than in 2024. Marshall beat Hamilton here 1,468 to 379, a margin of 57 points, after Trump carried the county by 71. That shift of about 15 points toward the Democrats was smaller than in most of Kansas, where every county moved left, the typical one by 18 points, and Hamilton won statewide. Rooks ranked 83rd of 105. Similar Republican counties moved between 11 and 18 points. Nationally, the typical county moved 14.

Turnout fell sharply: 1,922 votes were cast, 76% of the 2,534 cast in 2024. With that many fewer voters, the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20103.t:

That 22-point move toward the Democrats roughly matched the state's 21-point swing and beat the typical Kansas county (18 points) and the national typical move (14). It ranks 16th of 105 Kansas counties by move. Similar counties moved by comparable amounts: Crawford by 24 points, Harvey and Saline by 17 each.

Turnout fell sharply. The 28,360 votes cast were 78% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20017.t:
In the U.S. Senate race, Republican Roger Marshall carried Chase County over Democrat Adam Hamilton by 34 points, 753 votes to 365, out of 1,153 cast. That is 17 points closer than Donald Trump's 51-point margin here in 2024, a shift toward the Democrats nearly matching the typical Kansas county's 18-point move. Every one of the state's 105 counties moved left, and Hamilton won statewide by 5 points.

Turnout fell to 79% of the 2024 vote, so the count cannot tell voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home. Similar small, heavily Republican counties moved about as much: Pawnee by 15 points, Pratt by 18 and Ellsworth by 19. With 99% of the expected vote counted, these figures should hold.

Turnout fell sharply, to 444 votes from 593 in 2024, or 75% as many. The count therefore cannot separate voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home. Comparable small, deeply Republican counties moved less: Wichita by 15 points, Morton by 16 and Clark by 18.

20055.t:
Finney County swung hard toward the Democrats in the U.S. Senate race, flipping from a Trump county to a Hamilton one. Trump carried it by 35 points in 2024; Hamilton beat Marshall here 4,585 to 4,352, a 3-point margin, for a move of 37 points. That ranks third among Kansas's 105 counties, all of which moved left, and is about double both the typical Kansas county (+18) and the state as a whole (+21).

Neighboring comparisons split: Ford moved even more (+39) and also flipped, while Jefferson and Reno moved about 19 points and stayed Republican. Turnout was 86% of the 2024 level, 9,234 votes against 10,782, so the count cannot tell voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home.

20203.t:
In the U.S. Senate race, Wichita County backed Republican Roger Marshall over Democrat Adam Hamilton 538 to 128, a margin of 59 points. That is 15 points less Republican than the county's 74-point margin for Trump over Harris in 2024. Every Kansas county moved toward the Democrats, and this one moved less than most, ranking 84th of 105. The typical county in Kansas shifted 18 points, and statewide Hamilton won by 5 after Trump carried Kansas by 16.

Similar small counties moved further: Morton 16 points, Clark 18 and Greeley 27. Turnout here was 81% of 2024's 860 votes, so the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20043.t: In the U.S. Senate race between Hamilton and Marshall, Doniphan County stayed firmly Republican but moved about 16 points toward the Democrats. Trump carried it by 64 points in 2024; Marshall carried it by 48, with 1,839 votes to Hamilton's 610 out of 2,562 cast. Every Kansas county moved left, and Doniphan's shift was a little smaller than the typical county's 18 points, ranking 73rd of 105. It was also smaller than the statewide swing of 21 points but above the national typical move of 14. Similar counties moved alike: Wilson and Harper both shifted 16 points, and Mitchell 12. Turnout was only 72% of the 2024 vote, so the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20045.t:
Douglas County backed Democrat Adam Hamilton over Republican Roger Marshall by 54 points in the Senate race, 38,854 votes to 10,985. Harris had carried it by 38 points in 2024, so the county moved 17 points toward the Democrats. That is close to the typical Kansas county's shift of 18 points and a little less than the statewide move of 21. Every one of the state's 105 counties moved left, and Douglas ranks 61st by size of move.

About 50,926 votes were cast, 88% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot separate voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home. Among comparable counties, Wyandotte moved 25 points, Johnson 20 and Shawnee 19.

20057.t:
Ford County swung hard in the U.S. Senate race. Trump carried it by 38 points in 2024, but Democrat Hamilton edged Republican Marshall by about a point, 3,520 to 3,443. That is a 39-point move toward the Democrats, second-largest of Kansas's 105 counties and roughly double the state's 21-point shift. Ford is one of six Kansas counties that went from a Trump win to a Democratic win.

Counties that voted much like Ford in 2024 moved far less. Labette, Jefferson and Atchison shifted 19 to 23 points and stayed Republican. About 7,198 votes were cast, 88% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot tell who changed their mind from who stayed home.

20165.t:
In the U.S. Senate race, Rush County stayed firmly with Republican Roger Marshall, who beat Democrat Adam Hamilton 922 to 326, a margin of 46 points. That is still lopsided, but it is 20 points narrower than Trump's 65-point win here in 2024. The shift was a little larger than the typical Kansas county's 18 points, ranking 30th of 105 in a state where every county moved left. It also outpaced similar counties such as Lincoln (10 points), Edwards (12) and Graham (17).

Turnout fell to 1,304 votes, 81% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot tell voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home.

20195.t:
In the U.S. Senate race between Hamilton and Marshall, Trego County stayed firmly Republican but swung toward the Democrats. Trump carried it by 71 points in 2024; Marshall won it by 53, with 1,001 votes to Hamilton's 276. That 18-point move almost exactly matches the typical Kansas county (also 18) and ranks 52nd of 105, while every county in the state moved left. It also ran ahead of the typical national move of 14 points. Similar small Republican counties varied: Meade moved 18, Logan 15 and Chautauqua 11.

Turnout fell to 1,359 votes, 86% of the 2024 total, so the count cannot tell voters who changed their minds from those who stayed home.
